tip: 'Dag' by itself means both hi and bye, an informal greeting or farewell, besides being the word for day.
With 'geven' the receiver can come first with no preposition: 'wij geven de kinderen hun eten'.
After 'een' with a het-word the adjective takes no -e: 'een nieuw huis' ('het huis'), not 'nieuwe'.
'Aan het' plus an infinitive is the action-in-progress form: 'wat ben je aan het doen'.
'Wat leuk om ... te ...' is the pattern for a pleased reaction: 'wat leuk om je hier te zien' = how nice to see you here.
'Zal ik ...?' is how you offer to do something: 'zal ik je even een handje helpen?' = shall I give you a hand?
'Opbellen' is separable; in a main clause 'op' moves to the end: 'hij belt zijn moeder elke zondag op'.
When the item comes first, mark the receiver with 'aan': 'ik geef het boek aan mijn vriend'.
Dutch often uses the present tense for future plans: 'ik bel je morgenvroeg' means I will call you.
'Graag' with 'wil' softens it into a polite 'would like': 'ik wil graag een kopje koffie bestellen'.
Present tense plus 'al' covers duration up to now: 'woont u al' = have you been living.
Dutch usually picks a posture verb for location: 'de kleine kat zit op de warme bank' uses 'zit', not 'is'.
Clock times take 'om ... uur': 'om zes uur' = at six o'clock.
After a modal like 'kun', a separable verb stays joined at the end: 'terugbellen' stays in one piece.
'Als' starts a sub-clause, so its verb goes to the end: 'als je klaar bent', not 'als je bent klaar'.
'Aan het' plus an infinitive marks an action in progress: 'ik was net aan je aan het denken' = I was just thinking about you.
'Wat een' plus a noun makes an exclamation: 'wat een gedoe' = what a hassle.
The 'is being done' form uses 'worden' plus a past participle: 'het gebouw wordt gesloopt' = is being demolished.
'Trots' takes 'op' for the thing you are proud of: 'trots op wat je hebt bereikt'.
'Ons' is the form of our used with het-words: 'ons restaurant' ('het restaurant'); de-words take 'onze'.
'Hoeven' pairs with a negative to mean 'don't have to': 'de kinderen hoeven vandaag niet naar school'.
A decision is taken in Dutch: 'een beslissing nemen', not 'maken'.
'Wat betreft' opens a topic, like English 'as for': 'wat betreft de planning'.
Purpose is built with 'om ... te' plus an infinitive: 'om het contract te bespreken'.
'Weggooien' (to throw away) is separable; 'gooi' comes second and 'weg' lands at the very end.
'Hoe ..., hoe ...' means the more, the more: 'hoe harder het waait, hoe hoger de golven'.
'Afscheid nemen van' = to say goodbye to, literally to take leave of.
'Oranje' never takes an -e ending, unlike most adjectives: 'dikke' takes -e here, but 'oranje' stays unchanged.
A modal like 'mag' pushes the main verb to the end: 'mag je niet roken', with 'roken' last.
Start with 'natuurlijk' and the verb comes second, so subject and verb swap: 'wil ik', not 'ik wil'.
